options: Attaining moral perfection by mastering thirteen virtues one at a time
Founding a printing business with thirteen apprentices in Philadelphia
Writing a dictionary of virtues drawn from Greek philosophers
Organizing a debating club to practice thirteen rules of conversation
questions.explain: He set out to live without fault, using thirteen virtues and a daily examination method.

questions.q: What is the precept for Temperance?
options: Speak not but what may benefit others
Lose no time; be always employ'd in something useful
Eat not to dullness; drink not to elevation
Let all your things have their places
questions.explain: Temperance: 'Eat not to dullness; drink not to elevation.'

questions.q: Why did Franklin put Silence second?
options: To please his employer by speaking less in the print shop
To listen more and learn, and break a habit of prattling
To avoid quarrels with his brother over money and debt
To save money on candles by working in silence each night
questions.explain: He wanted to gain knowledge by listening and to break his habit of prattling, punning and joking.

questions.q: How did he record faults in his little book?
options: Black spots in ruled columns for each day and virtue
Red ink checkmarks in a daily ledger of successes
Written essays each night on the faults of the day
Letters sent each week to friends listing his errors
questions.explain: Pages were ruled with red ink into seven day columns, thirteen virtue lines, marked with black spots for faults.

questions.q: Why did Franklin conclude he needed a method rather than simple conviction?
options: His friends told him that reading about virtue was the surest cure
Knowing virtue is in our interest wasn't enough; habits had to change
He lacked knowledge of right and wrong, so rules were needed
He believed no one could be virtuous without a strict teacher
questions.explain: He found habit and inclination overpowered reason, so contrary habits must be broken and good ones established.
